newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Ex-government forces roll back Afghan Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Ex-government forces roll back Afghan Taleban.

text.p: Former Afghan government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood has rolled back the Taleban militia that drove him from Kabul two weeks ago, taking two towns and possibly further territory, reliable sources said on Sunday.
They said Jabal-os-Saraj, the Taleban front-line headquarters town at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains and a two-hour drive from Kabul, fell on Saturday.
Masood then captured Charikar, a 30-minute drive south of Jabal-os-Saraj, after a fierce five-hour battle later in the day, the sources said.

The sources, who asked not to be identified, said the road town of Qarah Bagh, a 40-minute drive north of the capital, was empty and that forces of the mostly ethnic Pushtun Taleban were massing to the south of it.
It was not clear if Masood's forces were near Qarah Bagh but the sources said people in Charikar were expecting a counter-attack.

Taleban officials in Kabul strenuously denied losing any territory, but fighters said the second road north was closed to civilian traffic at the outskirts of the capital because Masood's largely ethnic Tajik men were in hills above it.
They said Bagram, the government's main airbase 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, was still under Taleban control but there was fighting around it.

But Masood's advance, less than a week after ending the Taleban siege of his Panjsher Valley fortress by launching an attack in the Salang Pass, was a stunning reversal for a militia that had swept all before it in two years of existence.

"Everything will now depend on Taleban morale," said one veteran Afghan watcher in Kabul. "Can they reorganize and push Masood back again? We don't know because they've never faced a situation like this."
The Taleban have taken power in about three-quarters of Afghanistan since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan.

But Masood, who won a reputation as one of the country's best guerrilla generals with his defences of the Panshjer against Soviet troops in the 1980s when Moscow backed a communist government, has them rattled now.

In addition to his push down the main road from the Salang, he has also orchestrated a series of hit-and-run attacks well behind the front lines, some of them as close as 15 km (nine miles) from Kabul.
He sent envoys to local commanders who had joined the Taleban and pursuaded them to return to his side and these fighters cut the road below Qarah Bagh, local people said.
Masood's own forces pounded Bagram and appear to control most of the area around it and witnesses say the Taleban have sent in several air strikes in a bid to dislodge them.

The attacks, reminiscent of his tactics in the 1980s, have clearly got the Taleban worried. In sharp contrast to genial conversations with reporters earlier, some Taleban on the road have become aggressive.

Afghan watchers in Kabul said that was a sure sign the tide had turned against the Taleban north of Kabul, but that it was unlikely Masood could retake the city without the backing of northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum.

He signed a military pact with the Uzbek chief earlier this week, promising to help him unless fighting stopped, but there have not yet been any signs on the ground that Dostum's men were involved directly in the fighting.
"But Masood has suprised us before and he might again," said one Afghan watcher.
